---
title: "how do children think about coordinating collective life?"
description: "the development of cognition about collective life"
---

::: {.lede}
Human life is collective life. From families to classrooms to nations, we depend on groups to
accomplish what no individual could do alone — but coordinating a group poses problems that are
different in kind from navigating an interaction with a single partner.
:::

Knowing what one person wants, knows, or intends is not enough to get by in a group. Groups must
reconcile competing interests, decide who has a say, and agree on rules that guide everyone. Adults
inherit a rich toolkit for these problems, from voting to drawing lots. My research asks how
children come to understand that toolkit — and, more broadly, how people learn to see rules and
procedures as legitimate. I study this developmentally because childhood is a particularly useful
window: children meet disagreement, hierarchy, and group decision-making long before they receive
any formal instruction in procedure, so their judgments reveal which expectations emerge early and
which are revised through experience.

## 1 · reasoning about individuals and rules

::: {.strand-q}
Who is this, and how will they act?
:::

One way to navigate social life is to work out who other people are and anticipate how they will
act. I have found that children generalize dominance relationships across contexts to predict who
will prevail in future conflicts, but do not generalize submissiveness the same way — power, but
not deference, is treated as a property that travels with a person. I have also studied how
children draw moral conclusions from the way people condemn wrongdoing, treating condemnation as a
costly signal of the condemner's own commitments.

A third strand extends this reasoning to rules themselves. Principles like equality, merit, and
turn-taking can supply genuine reasons for a decision, but they can also be invoked strategically —
favoring equality when equality pays, then switching to merit when merit does instead. I examine
when children begin to distinguish principled from self-serving rule use, and when they use a
person's procedural choices to predict how that person will behave later.

::: {.cites .s1}
[Representative publications]{.cites-label}

- Hok, H.\*, Vasquez, K.\*, Barakzai, A., & Shaw, A. (2024). [The nonmeek inherit the earth: Children generalize dominance, but not submissiveness](https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0001696). *Developmental Psychology, 60*(7), 1187.
- Hok, H., Martin, A., Trail, Z., & Shaw, A. (2020). [When children treat condemnation as a signal: The costs and benefits of condemnation](https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.13323). *Child Development, 91*(5), 1439–1455.
- Hok, H., & Shaw, A. What's fair is unfair: Children's beliefs about the flexible use of impartial decision-rules. *Psychological Science*. [Under revision.]{.note}
- [Related collaborative work]{.related-tag} Santhanagopalan, R., Hok, H., Shaw, A., & Kinzler, K. D. (2025). [The ontogeny of attitudes toward migrants](https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.13599). *Developmental Science, 28*(2), e13599.

## 2 · group decision-procedures

::: {.strand-q}
Who decides, and by what rule?
:::

Knowing what each person will do does not settle what a group should do when its members disagree.
Groups need decision rules that aggregate preferences without deferring to any one person. Across
four experiments with 4- to 9-year-olds in the United States and China, children preferred majority
rule to letting a single individual decide by age four, and preferred it to a coin flip — a
procedure they already regard as fair — by age six. Their endorsement was not indiscriminate:
majority rule was appropriate for settling shared preferences, like what a group should eat or do
together, but not for dictating an individual's personal choice or legitimizing clearly immoral
behavior. Children do not treat majorities as a brute social force; they show an early,
context-sensitive understanding of procedural legitimacy.

Two further questions surround the vote itself. First, whose preferences count? Comparing
universalist voting to systems restricted to experts or to morally good decision-makers, both
children and adults preferred systems in which everyone had a voice, and judged them fairer even
when exclusion might be more effective — though older participants more readily acknowledged
exclusion's potential benefits. Second, how costly is agreement to reach? Children pick up on
structural coordination costs early: by age six they expect larger groups, and groups split among
more competing positions, to take longer to decide.

::: {.cites .s2}
[Representative publications]{.cites-label}

- Hok, H., Gerdin, E., Zhao, X., & Shaw, A. (2025). [When should the majority rule? Children's developing intuitions about majority rules voting](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2025.106128). *Cognition, 260*, 106128.
- Hok, H., Silva, G., Shaw, A., & Yang, F. (2026). [Who should have a voice? Children's evaluations of universalist versus exclusive voting](https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0001795). *Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 155*(1), 94.
- Richardson, E., Hok, H., Shaw, A., & Keil, F. C. (2025). [Herding cats: Children and adults infer collective decision speed from team size and diversity](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2025.106211). *Cognition, 263*, 106211.
:::

## 3 · formalizing rules

::: {.strand-q}
When must norms become explicit?
:::

Most social norms are never written down; they are sustained through shared understandings members
are expected to recognize. Formal rules seem to matter when those understandings stop being
sufficient. Across five experiments, adults and children judged which groups would adopt formal
rules and what problems those rules would solve. Adults expected formalization in larger and more
diverse groups, in groups marked by internal disagreement, and among members who were less socially
close — but not merely in response to external hardship like disaster or scarcity. Their
expectations were best predicted by judgments that a group faced social-dynamic problems, such as
weak shared assumptions about what a norm requires, rather than problems of individual misbehavior
alone. Children ages 8 to 11 connected formal rules to these same problems, differentiating less
sharply among them.

This points to what I find most interesting about written rules: their double life. A formal rule is
a tool for future coordination, but it is also a trace of a group's history. Children and adults
alike infer more past rule-breaking, yet less present rule-breaking, where a rule has been made
explicit.

::: {.cites .s3}
[Representative publications]{.cites-label}

- Hok, H., Thomas, A. J., & Saxe, R. (2025). [Written in stone: Lay intuitions about the emergence of formal rules](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/8tf7j3v5). *Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society, 47*.
- Hok, H., Saxe, R., & Thomas, A. J. (2026). US children and adults infer higher past rule-breaking, but lower present rule-breaking, in the presence of formal rules. *Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society, 48*.
:::

## what comes next

My next line of work brings these questions into live peer interaction. Much of developmental social
cognition relies on controlled vignettes, dyadic tasks, or observation of naturally occurring
conflict — approaches that make it hard to study the conditions under which group-level procedures
actually become necessary. Working with SchoolSpace.io, an educational platform hosting more than
100,000 students in digital classrooms, I am developing paradigms in which children ages 4 to 6 and
8 to 10 make decisions together synchronously while I vary group size, familiarity, and preference
conflict. The prediction follows directly from the formalization work: when children are few,
familiar, and aligned, interpersonal knowledge suffices and they can negotiate case by case; as
groups grow larger and less familiar, procedures that treat members interchangeably become more
valuable.

Across all of this work, my goal is to explain how children come to understand collective life as
something people make, not simply something they inherit.

::: {.secondary}
[Additional lines of work]{.eyebrow}

Two collaborative strands run alongside the core program and share its central concern — how
fairness and coordination work when the participants are not simply familiar peers.

## children's fairness toward robots and machines

If children's fairness judgments depend on who — or what — is receiving a resource, then robots are
a useful test case. In collaboration with researchers in human-robot interaction, I study when
children think it is acceptable to give a robot less than a human peer, and how those judgments
compare to judgments about inanimate objects like toys. This work asks what children take a robot to
be for purposes of fair distribution, and connects the developmental literature on fairness to
practical questions about how children will treat the social machines they increasingly grow up
with.

::: {.cites}
[Representative publications]{.cites-label}

- Ayalon, O., Hok, H., Shaw, A., & Gordon, G. (2023). [When it is ok to give the robot less: Children's fairness intuitions towards robots](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12369-023-01047-4). *International Journal of Social Robotics, 15*(9), 1581–1601.
- Ayalon, O., Hok, H., Shaw, A., & Gordon, G. (2026). [From children to toy trucks, and robots too: Exploring children's fairness perceptions](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chbr.2026.101136). *Computers in Human Behavior Reports, 22*, 101136.
:::

## open science, metascience, and digital scholarship

Scientific communities face the same coordination problems I study in children's groups: they need
norms, procedures, and infrastructure to produce trustworthy knowledge together. Through the Center
for Research in Equitable and Open Scholarship at MIT Libraries and related collaborations, I work
on how the systems through which knowledge is produced and shared can become more transparent,
equitable, and useful — surveying researchers' support for open science practices, developing
quality-control methods for curating 3D and immersive research data, evaluating AI tools in
educational settings, and analyzing political discourse across online platforms. I am particularly
interested in the role university libraries can play in this work.
